Discerner
dih-SUR-nur
n. (one that distinguishes or judges; a title given to the word of God)
From Latin discernere, to separate or distinguish — dis-, apart, and cernere, to sift or separate. It renders Greek kritikos, able to judge, from which we have critic: the word of God is the critic, and the reader is the text.

Biblical Definition

Hebrews calls the word of God quick and powerful, sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart. The Greek is kritikos. Scripture is the critic; we are not its reviewers. The image is surgical and uncomfortable: a blade that goes past where any human blade stops, through the seam where soul and spirit are joined, into the marrow of a man's motives, and distinguishes his thoughts from his intents — what he considered from what he actually meant. The next verse drops the figure and names the surgeon: all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do. Discernment therefore runs one direction before it runs the other. A man cannot judge the word, because the word is already judging him; and he cannot judge himself accurately, because the heart is deceitful above all things — it is the LORD who searches it. Only after that does Scripture ask believers to discern: to try the spirits, to prove all things, to have senses exercised to discern both good and evil. That discernment is a trained faculty, and it is trained by the blade.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): one that discerns, distinguishes, perceives or judges; one who sees or discriminates with accuracy.

expand to see more

DISCERNER, n. One that discerns, distinguishes, perceives or judges.

DISCERN, v.t. To separate by the eye or by the understanding; to distinguish; to make a difference between.

DISCERNMENT, n. The power or faculty of the mind by which it distinguishes one thing from another; acuteness of judgment.

INTENT, n. Design; purpose; drift; aim; that which is intended.

MARROW, n. A soft, oleaginous substance contained in the cavities of animal bones; the inner and best part.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 4:12 — "For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart."

Hebrews 4:13 — "Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do."

1 Corinthians 2:14 — "But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned."

Jeremiah 17:10 — "I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings."

Modern Corruption

Discernment is reduced to personal intuition — a feeling about a teacher or a book — while Scripture makes the word itself the discerner and the believer the one discerned before he discerns anything.

expand to see more

Two opposite failures share one root. The first calls suspicion discernment: a hard eye, a ready verdict, a ministry of detecting error in others that never turns the blade inward. Hebrews orders the operation the other way. The sword is in God's hand, the marrow being divided is mine, and the first fruit of real discernment is a man who has been found out. The second failure calls impression discernment: I sensed something, I had a check in my spirit, offered as evidence and treated as unanswerable. John gives an objective test instead — try the spirits whether they are of God, and the test is a confession about Christ come in the flesh, not a feeling in the room.

Paul adds the limit that keeps discernment humble. The natural man cannot receive the things of the Spirit of God, because they are spiritually discerned — the faculty is not native to fallen men and cannot be acquired by education or sharpened by cynicism. It is given with the Spirit and exercised by use: strong meat belongs to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil. So discernment grows the way a palate grows, on a steady diet of the word that is doing the discerning.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kritikos (G2924), able to judge or discern; enthumesis (G1761), a thought or deliberation; ennoia (G1771), intent or purpose; anakrino (G350), to examine or discern.

expand to see more

Greek kritikos (G2924) — skilled in judging; used once, and of the word of God rather than of a man.

Greek enthumesis (G1761) — what a man turns over in his mind; rendered thoughts.

Greek ennoia (G1771) — the settled intention behind the thought; rendered intents.

Greek anakrino (G350) — to sift, to examine judicially; he that is spiritual judgeth all things.

Greek trachelizo (G5136) — to lay bare the neck; the vivid verb behind opened in the next verse.

Usage

"“a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart” — the word as critic."

"“all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him” — the figure dropped, the person named."

"“because they are spiritually discerned” — the faculty is not natural."
